item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — There was no hangover at Uniqlo Field at Dodger Stadium.
Not after clinching the National League West. Not with the champagne still fresh in the Dodgers’ minds. And certainly not with Josue De Paula getting his first real taste of the big stage in Chavez Ravine.
Instead, the Dodgers looked very much like a team preparing for October. And De Paula looked like a player who wants to be part of it.
The 21-year-old came through with the go-ahead RBI double in the sixth inning Friday night, turning a tie game into a Dodgers lead and helping spark what eventually became an 8-2 victory over the Giants.
“It felt amazing,” De Paula said. “To do that for the team, give us the lead. I’m just celebrating with the boys. I just want to see us win.”
That last part might have been the most telling.
De Paula isn't approaching his first week in the major leagues like a player trying to prove he belongs with a franchise full of veterans and established stars. At least publicly, he's approaching it like a kid soaking in every moment.
But his performance is making it increasingly difficult for the Dodgers to ignore what he might bring when the calendar flips to October.
Dave Roberts acknowledged as much after the game.
“He’s certainly doing a lot of things well,” Roberts said when asked about De Paula potentially being part of the Dodgers’ postseason roster mix.
For now, De Paula says he's trying not to look too far ahead.
“Yeah, it’s crossed my mind,” he said of making the postseason roster. “Like I said, I try to focus on the now, right here. I’m enjoying every moment with these veteran players.”
The now, on Friday, was pretty impressive.
De Paula came to the plate in the fifth inning with the Dodgers trailing 2-1 and opened the frame with a single, his first hit at Dodger Stadium.
Mookie Betts followed with a single of his own, and Teoscar Hernández brought De Paula home with an RBI single to tie the game.
One inning later, De Paula was back in the middle of it.
This time, he delivered the biggest swing of the night to that point, lining an RBI double to put the Dodgers ahead.
A player who had spent years dreaming about moments like this had just created one.
“It was awesome,” De Paula said of his first week in the majors. “Like I said, everybody, the manager, all the teammates have been amazing and accepting me.”
There is, however, one part of his game De Paula knows still needs work.
His defense. And he's not shying away from it.
“I know that's a big area and improvement for me,” De Paula said. “I know I got a lot of hate on it. So I'm that type: if I get hate on it, I'm gonna focus on it more. So I'm gonna shut a lot of people up with my defense very soon.”
That confidence is unmistakable.
So is the willingness to accept criticism and use it as motivation.
The Dodgers don't need De Paula to become a finished product overnight. They need to determine whether his offensive impact, approach and overall upside give them enough reason to keep him around as they prepare for a postseason run.
And his teammates are already noticing what he does at the plate.
Betts, who knows something about making an impression in a Dodgers uniform, spoke highly of De Paula's at-bats.
“He's swinging at strikes, taking balls, impacting the ball,” Betts said. “There's no matchup that is really a bad matchup, which is really neat to see someone so young that can handle it…. He's been awesome.”
That might be the most encouraging part of De Paula's arrival.
The results are one thing. The at-bats are another.
He's not simply getting by on raw talent. He's showing an ability to recognize strikes, lay off pitches outside the zone and impact the baseball against major-league pitching.
And on a night when the Dodgers needed a spark, he provided it.
Of course, De Paula wasn't the only Dodger putting on a show.
Betts got the night started with a leadoff home run in the first inning, crushing the second pitch he saw from Giants left-hander Cesar Perdomo, a 93 mph fastball, into the left-field pavilion.
It was the 33rd leadoff home run of Betts' career.
Later, after the Giants briefly took control, Betts came back with another home run in the eighth inning, his second of the night and his 22nd of the season.
That's two more home runs than he hit last season, with eight games remaining.
Max Muncy and Kyle Tucker then went back-to-back, before Will Smith joined the party.
Four Dodgers, Muncy, Tucker, Betts and Smith, homered in the eighth inning.
What began as a competitive game suddenly became a rout. Muncy's home run gave him 29 for the season, while Tucker continued to show signs of heating up at precisely the time the Dodgers want their lineup clicking.
But none of that changes what made Friday night particularly interesting.
The Dodgers already know what Betts, Muncy, Tucker and Smith can do. They are still learning what De Paula can become.
And on his first night in the big-league spotlight at Uniqlo Field at Dodger Stadium, he gave them another reason to keep watching.
Tyler Glasnow did his part, too.
After Betts gave the Dodgers an early 1-0 lead, Glasnow surrendered a solo home run to Jung Hoo Lee in the second inning before Jonah Cox's RBI single put San Francisco ahead in the third.
From there, Glasnow settled down.
He finished with six innings, allowing three hits and two runs while walking two and striking out 10 on 98 pitches, 63 of them for strikes.
The bullpen took it from there, while the Dodgers' offense eventually turned a close game into another comfortable victory.
They are now 94-60 on the season and remain two games behind Milwaukee for the top seed in the National League, while building a four-game cushion over Atlanta for third place.
The division has already been won. The real work is beginning now.
De Paula says he's focused on the present.
The Dodgers, meanwhile, have to be thinking about the future.
Because if Friday was any indication, Josue De Paula isn't simply here to experience the major leagues.
He's here to make it increasingly difficult to send him anywhere else.

That's one way to start off the last homestand of the regular season.
Forget the fact that it was against the lowly San Francisco Giants and their lineup featuring a who's who of ... "Who?" Forget the fact that five of the Los Angeles Dodgers' runs in their dominant 8-2 win on Friday night came off the relatively unknown Philip Abner. The Dodgers' lineup, without Shohei Ohtani, showed exactly what they're capable of offensively.
This is the version of the team Andrew Friedman envisioned when he signed Kyle Tucker to a four-year, $240 million contract and Edwin Díaz to a three-year, $69 million deal last winter.
"The talent," manager Dave Roberts said. "It's a high-floor talent level. I just like the way we're taking better team at-bats and making up for not having Shohei in there. Obviously, we're a better team with him, but it is nice to see there hasn't been a drop-off with him not in the lineup."
Here's a look at three winners from the Dodgers' victory over the Giants:
The Dodgers lineup is just fine
Mookie Betts started things off when he jumped on a low-90s fastball that San Francisco starter Cesar Perdomo left middle-middle and sent it over the fence in left center field for his 33rd leadoff home run as a Dodger. The bats went quiet briefly from there until the bottom of the fifth when Teoscar Hernández singled home Josue De Paula from third on a sharp liner to right field to tie the game at 2-2.
The rookie De Paula later drove in the go-ahead run on an RBI double in the sixth before a monster five-run eighth inning in which Max Muncy, Tucker, Betts and Will Smith all went yard to put the game out of reach.
"I think that's the beauty in it," Betts said. "We just keep giving ourselves opportunities and eventually, something will crack. It did tonight, so we just have to keep getting guys on base and giving ourselves the chances and the hits will follow."
Edwin Díaz looked good in return from IL
That set the stage for the trumpets to once again blare over the Dodger Stadium loudspeakers. Roberts said he wouldn't have put Díaz in if it wasn't for the six-run lead as he wanted to give Díaz some leeway in his first outing back from an IL stint after health and poor performance have plagued his season.
But Díaz took the opportunity and ran with it. In his first big league appearance since Aug. 17, he got two quick outs before giving up a base hit up the middle. Rather than let that snowball like it has many times in 2026, however, Díaz was able to buckle down and strike out Brett Harris on three pitches to seal a Dodgers win.
"I liked everything," Roberts said. "I liked his intensity; I liked the fastball velocity. The slider was good. It was just really good to get him back in the mix and that's something to build on."
Josue De Paula is different
The through line for the offense on Friday night was the 21-year-old De Paula. The No. 6 prospect in baseball according to MLB Pipeline finished the night 2-for-3 with a walk, two runs and an RBI, but it was the timing of each of those that made his Dodger Stadium debut so special.
De Paula led off the bottom of the fifth with a base hit, which Betts followed up with one of his own before he eventually scored the tying run on Hernández's RBI single. Two innings later, De Paula scored Tucker from first on a double that he put on a rope at 107 mph deep into the right field gap. As he reached second, De Paula pounded his chest and flexed.
Then, in that huge eighth inning, it was De Paula who kept it alive by working a four-pitch walk with two outs, his seventh in a week in the big leagues. Five pitches later, Betts blew the game open with a two-run homer.
"I just love his at-bats," Roberts said. "It's one of those things that we knew coming up to the big leagues, he wasn't going to get overwhelmed, and it just helps when you control the strike zone. He takes his walks, when the ball is in the hitting zone, he can slug you but he also knows how to get a base hit. It's been very professional."

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers surge late to beat Giants as they work to get healthy for playoffs
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- Tyler Glasnow gives up three hits, two runs and strikes out 10 over six innings in the Dodgers’ 8-2 win over the San Francisco Giants.
- The Dodgers hit four home runs in the eighth inning, including a pair of back-to-back homers. Mookie Betts finished with two home runs.
With eight games left in the regular season, the Dodgers have already ticked off the most important boxes on their postseason to-do list.
They clinched a playoff berth for a record-tying 14th straight season and won the division title for the fifth time in a row. And with Friday’s 8-2 victory over the San Francisco Giants, the Dodgers (94-60) also have an outside shot at their fourth 100-win season in six years.
But that doesn’t mean they don’t have a lot of work to do between now and the start of the playoffs — the most important task being determining exactly where and when they’ll open the postseason.
With Friday’s win and the Milwaukee Brewers’ victory in Baltimore, the Dodgers trail the Brewers by two games in the race for the league’s best record and the home-field advantage in the postseason that goes with it. They also lead the Atlanta Braves by four games for the league’s second-best record, which would give them a first-round playoff bye and an extra five days to get their sizable contingent of walking wounded healthy.
The magic is indeed missing, and after two seasons of conjuring up postseason greatness, these back-to-reality Dodgers appear headed for an early fall.
“To get one of these top two seeds is important. And our guys understand that,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “Winning the division is great, but I still think our best baseball is ahead of us.”
Achieving that, however, will require emptying an injury list that is almost as long as the team’s starting lineup. If the season ended today, the Dodgers would have at least seven players who wouldn’t be ready to play.
The Dodgers are also hopeful left-hander Blake Snell, who came out of Wednesday’s game after an inning with groin tightness, will be healthy enough to return for one more regular-season start.
Center fielder Andy Pages, who shares the team lead in RBIs with Shohei Ohtani despite missing a month with a fracture in his left hand, is expected to be activated for the series against the San Diego Padres, which begins Tuesday, while backup catcher Dalton Rushing is swinging a bat and will hit against a pitching machine this weekend.
Right-hander Roki Sasaki threw 48 pitches in a bullpen session Wednesday and could come off the IL next week but right-hander Edgardo Henriquez, second among Dodger relievers in innings and strikeouts, will miss the rest of the regular season with a back strain. He could join the team for the playoffs.
Then there’s Ohtani, the four-time MVP. He’s dealing with injuries to his left knee and right biceps. He has resumed taking batting practice and is eligible to come off the IL Wednesday. Roberts said he hopes to get Ohtani 10-12 at-bats before the playoffs.
“I’m just really waiting to hear when he’s going to get on the field, let alone take live BP,” Roberts said. “He’s not there yet. But everything I’ve heard, it’s been a really productive last three to four to five days.”
One player who did return was closer Edwin Díaz. Limited by multiple injuries to just 16 appearances this season, he was activated off the injured list Friday and threw 17 pitches in the ninth, giving up a single and striking out two batters.
For Roberts, the last month has looked like an episode of “The Pitt,” with medical crises piling up, one atop the other. Yet that’s hardly slowed the Dodgers, who opened their final homestand of the season having won 11 of their past 14 games.
Now the focus becomes continuing that momentum while getting as close to full strength as possible.
“They can go hand in hand,” Roberts said. “We have a lot of good players that are more than capable of helping us win baseball games, at the same time making sure we try to get our best players to optimum health when the postseason starts.”
The Dodgers got a big lift Friday from rookie Josue De Paula, a player who didn’t figure in their postseason plans until a week ago, when he was called up to take Ohtani’s place. In his Dodger Stadium debut, De Paula singled and scored on a Teoscar Hernández single in the fifth, then roped a double to the wall in right-center an inning later, scoring Kyle Tucker to put the Dodgers ahead to stay.
Tucker, Max Muncy, Mookie Betts and Will Smith all homered in a five-run eighth inning, turning a nail-biter into a comfortable win.
Dodgers owner Mark Walter and multiple insurance companies he owns are being sued for allegedly failing to disclose an ongoing federal probe to customers.
That gave right-hander Tyler Glasnow (5-1) his second win since April 23. Glasnow gave up just three hits in six innings, striking out a season-high 10 batters.
Hernández, who had two hits, is batting .368 with 17 RBIs in September; Tucker, who also had two hits, is hitting .424 with five home runs and 13 runs scored in his past 10 games; while Betts, with two homers Friday, has six hits in his past eight at-bats, lifting his average to a season-high .254.
That’s helped make up for Freddie Freeman’s struggles. Freeman, who went hitless in four at-bats Friday, striking out twice, has just six hits — and 13 strikeouts — in his last 48 at-bats.
“We still have a lot of work to do,” Roberts said before the game.
They have just over a week left to get it done.

CINCINNATI — As the celebrating Los Angeles Dodgers drenched one another in various carbonated boozes, the team's most important character was bone dry and most likely quite sober roughly two thousand miles away.
Shohei Ohtani, that baseballing mover of mountains, is injured. A laundry list of ailing body parts — biceps, knee, neck — first kept the two-way dynamo from pitching, then frayed his offensive impact and finally rendered him physically incapable of taking the field. Last week, the Dodgers placed him on the IL, with just a few weeks left for him to recover before the start of the postseason and only five games between his earliest eligible return date and the end of the regular season.
Publicly, the club has maintained an optimistic tone, describing his issues as manageable, not season-ending. A return before the end of the regular season is still in play, skipper Dave Roberts reaffirmed this week. Yet nobody around the game would be shocked if the Dodgers opt for caution and keep Ohtani sidelined until October. Los Angeles' worst-case scenario, of course, would be a postseason without its main man.
So when the Dodgers embarked on their recent two-city swing, their $700 million slugger stayed back in Southern California. He rested, received treatment and hit off a tee — or, as Roberts vaguely put it, "continued his progression."
"Overall, [his] body feels normal-ish," Roberts said before Thursday's clincher. "Then it's kind of getting his body, his knee, his arm, biceps, whatever, back to full strength."
This marked the first time in the Dodgers' Ohtani Era that the man himself did not accompany the team for the entirety of a road trip. In fact, the most recent occurrence of a Dodgers club flying home without Ohtani came in October 2023, after the team's sweep loss to the Diamondbacks in that year's NLDS. Lance Lynn, Austin Barnes and a decade of frustration were on board that plane. Ohtani was still technically an Angel. In other words, it's been a while.
With the two-way superstar now the center of the Dodgers' solar system — and, to a large extent, the league's extended universe — Ohtani's absence this week in Cincinnati was easy to sense, impossible to avoid. Throughout the week, all about the yard, were reminders both big and small.
The blue bat bags lined up outside the locker room in numerical order went right from Will Smith's No. 16 to Kyle Tucker's No. 23, with no No. 17 to be found. Dodgers head security guard Al Garcia, typically within eyesight of Ohtani at all times, floated around the clubhouse with an uncharacteristically laid-back comportment buoyed by his relatively light list of duties.
A group of passionate Dodgers fans recognized the star's absence with a homemade sign that read "Feel Better Shohei, Give Decoy A Hug," making reference to Ohtani's dog. Even Yoshinobu Yamamoto admitted that it was odd not having Ohtani around, delivering one of his funnier and more cutting lines of the season.
"It's been a weird feeling because I talk to him all the time in the clubhouse," Yamamoto said via interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda. "Although I have Roki [Sasaki], he doesn't really talk to me."
The Dodgers' lineup missed Ohtani, too, averaging less than four runs per game on the road trip before Thursday's eight-run outburst against a bottom-five Cincinnati pitching staff. Utilityman Tommy Edman got the bulk of leadoff duties, with Mookie Betts and rookie call-up Josue De Paula getting a day each in the one-hole. Edman went just 1-for-23 on the trip. Freddie Freeman's power dip continued, with five singles and nothing else. Will Smith has yet to really pop off since his return from the IL on Sept. 1.
"It feels different because he's such a presence when he's on the field," Roberts admitted Monday.
Therein lies the lingering concern. The Dodgers and Ohtani have all but accepted that he won't pitch again this season. That's not the end of the world; Los Angeles has the arms to solve that problem. On the other hand, navigating October without Ohtani at full-go would be a difficult proposition.
Ohtani's health, too, is not binary. Even if he plays, which at this point feels likely, he's unlikely to be completely healed. That dynamic could very well hamper his performance. Ohtani, overly cautious as they come, revealed that concern the last time he spoke to reporters on Sept. 8.
"I should have enough experience to address any kinks or injuries or anything like that with the swing," Ohtani said. "I'm going to use this as an opportunity to add on to the experience that I've had previously and address it regardless."
It's not exactly the most reassuring explanation — Ohtani implying that he'll need to manage his various discomforts for the rest of the season. How that process transpires and how productive Ohtani proves to be in October could determine how many Champagne celebrations he'll get to participate in this year.

Tanner Scott lanzó la novena para acreditarse su 22º salvamento.

They hit their magic number, but minus the magic.
The Dodgers trudged toward October by clinching their 13th National League West title in 14 years on Thursday, their customary march mired in a quicksand of questions.
Has any Dodger team during this golden era entered the playoffs with more injuries, more uncertainty, and a greater fear of underachievement?
Will the party in Cincinnati be the last time they celebrate this season?
The magic is indeed missing, and after two seasons of conjuring up postseason greatness, these back-to-reality Dodgers appear headed for an early fall.
The Three-Peat looks like a no-go.
Despite the best efforts from baseball’s best braintrust, their latest creation simply doesn’t have the appearance of a championship team.
They’re aging, they’re hurting and, with only a couple of weeks left until the beginning of their annual autumnal angst, they look tired and taut and unprepared for this monumental tussle with history.
“I think for me, the message was, ‘We haven’t come close to playing our best baseball yet.’” manager Dave Roberts told reporters when relaying his speech to the team earlier this week upon clinching a record-tying 14th consecutive playoff berth.
He added, “The message was, we’ve accomplished a lot up to this point, all the while not playing our best baseball. So let’s get some of these guys healthy.”
Haven’t come close to playing our best baseball… Let’s get some of these guys healthy.
Not exactly “Win one for the Gipper” stuff, but completely accurate. These postseason’s themes are more realistic than inspirational, and for good reason.
No, they haven’t come close to playing their best baseball. Forget what you see in these season-ending games against some of the worst teams. Remember, instead, what they’ve done against some of baseball’s best.
Since the All-Star break, they are 4-12 against the five National League playoff contenders. The Atlanta Braves swept them. The Chicago Cubs swept them. The Milwaukee Brewers dominated them.
These teams will be waiting for them in October, and even baseball’s richest roster might not be enough to carry this staggered bunch through their toughest stretch. They’ve played a lot of games in three years, all under baseball’s brightest spotlight, every night, scores of media, millions of fans, a worldwide whirl for 28 regular dudes, and it’s finally taken its toll.
They’ve hit the wall… and the wall is about to hit back.
“It’s not easy, I think it’s a lot harder than people think it is,” said Roberts. “Human nature alone, when you’re hungry, when you’re chasing something, it’s a lot more easy to be motivated, versus, having been there, done that, it gets a little trite, a little old.”
He added: “To keep guys enthusiastic, focused, hungry, that’s harder. But to their credit, they stayed the course. And for me, we’re just as hungry as we were in ‘24 and ‘25. This is a separate season. Our guys understand.”
The 1988-89 Lakers understood, too. And they still got burned in ways that Dodger fans will find painfully familiar. Showtime was chasing the original “three-peat” trademarked by Pat Riley when the Lakers were swept by the Detroit Pistons in a Finals that seemed cursed,
Byron Scott missed the series with a hamstring injury and Magic Johnson essentially missed the final two games with a hamstring injury and they couldn’t survive.
This looks like the Dodgers today. Their injuries feel too major, and the impact too deep.
Start with Shohei Ohtani. The Dodgers haven’t won a full-season championship in 38 years without him at the top of the lineup. He’ll be there again, but his body has been breaking down for the last couple of months, and, before being recently placed on the injured list — finally! — he was only a shadow of himself.
He hasn’t hit a home run or driven in a run outside of Coors Field in more than a month. In his last 24 games before going on the IL with biceps and knee issues, he was batting .198. The Dodgers can’t admit it, and Ohtani would never acknowledge it, but this is a man in serious need of an extended rest.
Teoscar Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday in the Dodgers’ win against the Reds was his second home run in as many nights.
Also on the injured list in these final days is Andy Pages, who was having a career year before breaking his hand. He’ll return without much time to get ready for October, and this is a man who will need some time, as he has a career .114 average in the postseason and was even benched last year before he redeemed himself with that picturesque catch over Kiké Hernández.
Speaking of last October’s heroes, the biggest savior has also spent the summer in pain, Will Smith battling neck issues until recently returning to the lineup. But the comeback has been bumpy. In his initial games since returning at the start of September, Smith was batting .171. Last October he set a major league record by catching 73 innings in the World Series. He is still paying the price.
Then there’s Freddie Freeman, whose bat doesn’t have the same pop, who’s step doesn’t have the same spring, and who has his worst OPS in 14 years. Add an inconsistent Mookie Betts and an incredibly streaky Teoscar Hernández to an already-shaky lineup.
It’s been such an unsteady year, Andrew Friedman’s two big offseason acquisitions have been busts. Edwin Díaz has been terrible, and then injured, then terrible again. Kyle Tucker has been terrible, then worse, then mostly invisible.
Even the Dodgers two role-playing heroes have seemingly disappeared. Kiké Hernández, at age 35, has his lowest home-run total — three — in 12 years. Miguel Rojas, at age 37, has his lowest home run and RBI totals in nine years.
The Dodgers clinch a playoff berth with their 4-1 victory over the Cincinnati Reds, reaching the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year.
As if they didn’t have enough problems on the field and at the plate, check out the mound. No, don’t.
Even what should be their strength is now being threatened. Blake Snell left Wednesday’s game early with groin issues and Tyler Glasnow recently complained of general discomfort. This leaves a proven playoff rotation of two, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tarik Skubal, and if you think Yamamoto threw a lot of innings last October, this time he won’t be able to leave the mound for a month.
In all, this is a Dodger team facing its toughest challenge yet, their quest for an historic three-peat much tougher than the last two journeys, one that will require arguably the greatest stretch of baseball in franchise history to complete.
This division title is a nice beginning.
It could also be the end.

The Los Angeles Dodgers brought third baseman Max Muncy and outfielder Josue De Paula back into the lineup for Thursday’s series finale against the Cincinnati Reds.
The Dodgers lost Wednesday’s game after Cy Young winner Blake Snell went down with a groin injury after pitching just one inning. Luckily, Snell believes he can still make a start before the end of the regular season, which ends in less than two weeks.
LA won the first two games of the series, shutting down a powerful Reds lineup, and will look to do the same to win the series Wednesday.
Who is Starting for the Dodgers?
Justin Wrobleski will start for the Dodgers on Wednesday, making his 25th appearance of the regular season. Two of his last three appearances have come out of the bullpen, and none of them have lasted more than three innings since his return from the injured list with a forearm problem.
He has a 3.78 ERA on the year, striking out 111 batters over the course of 133.1 innings—his heaviest workload in an MLB season so far.
How deep into the game he goes depends on him, but the Dodgers will have backup in the form of Landon Knack whenever Wrobleski is ready to come out.
Who is in the Dodgers’ Lineup?
The Dodgers still don’t have Shohei Ohtani in the lineup, but Tommy Edman has replaced him well and will play center field on Thursday. Freddie Freeman moves up a couple of spots into the No. 2 hole, followed by right fielder Kyle Tucker, who will bat third.
Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez takes over the cleanup spot, followed by Muncy, who slides back into third base and bats fifth. De Paula serves as the designated hitter and will bat sixth, with catcher Hunter Feduccia giving Will Smith an off day in the No. 7 spot.
Second baseman Alex Freeland will bat eight for the Dodgers, with Miguel Rojas rounding out the lineup and playing shortstop—giving Mookie Betts a well-deserved rest day.
Dodgers Lineup vs. Reds
1. Tommy Edman, CF
2. Freddie Freeman, 1B
3. Kyle Tucker, RF
4. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
5. Max Muncy, 3B
6. Josue De Paula, DH
7. Hunter Feduccia, C
8. Alex Freeland, 2B
9. Miguel Rojas, SS
P. Justin Wrobleski, LHP
Who is Starting for the Reds?
Veteran right-hander Brady Singer is starting for the Reds, making his 30th appearance of the season. He has reached that mark in each of the last three seasons, and has 25 or more appearances in all seven of his MLB campaigns bar 2020.
He isn’t having the best year despite his regular consistency, though, as he has a 5.38 ERA through 150.2 innings with only 125 strikeouts on the season.
Singer didn’t face the Dodgers in last week’s series in Los Angeles, but he has a pretty good track record against the team. In three appearances against LA, all of which came during his time with Kansas City, he has a 1.89 ERA through 19 innings with 15 strikeouts.
The Dodgers will hope to break that trend on Thursday as they look to bring themselves even closer to a first-round postseason bye. The first pitch of Thursday’s game comes at 9:40 p.m. PT.

The Los Angeles Dodgers lost to the Cincinnati Reds, 6-2, on Wednesday and fell to 92-60 on the year.
Blake Snell pitched just one inning before he was removed from his start due to groin tightness. After Blake Treinen pitched a clean second inning, the Reds took advantage of the impromptu bullpen game and halted any potential NL West-clinching celebrations.
Offensively, Mookie Betts still shined with a three-hit outing and Will Smith also enjoyed a multi-hit night. The backstop appears to be gaining his footing once again, hitting .273 with three RBIs in his last seven games.
Ahead of the eventual defeat, the Dodgers surprisingly designated an outfielder for assignment hitting .218 in his first 20 MLB games in order to make room on the roster to activate All-Star right-hander Kris Bubic. Though it wasn't the most ideal situation to be making his debut with the two-time defending champions, Bubic struck out two in a scoreless eighth inning.
After the game, both Snell and manager Dave Roberts provided an update on the left-hander's injury. Snell revealed that he felt his groin "grab" during a pregame bullpen and knew then he shouldn't go beyond the first inning. Regardless, he said he "should be good" to make another start before the postseason.
Roberts, however, wasn't as sure.
“It’s a possibility,” Roberts said. “I like where his head is at, but he just can’t afford any more setbacks. So, whether it’s his next start or being pushed back or whatever it is, we’ve got to make sure that he comes out ready to go in the postseason.”
Finally, right-hander and presumed closer Edwin Díaz doesn't appear to be making much progress amid his return from another injured list stint. Manager Dave Roberts, among others, was not happy with the results of his rehab outing over the weekend, and knows that at this moment, Díaz is not someone a World Series favorite wants in their bullpen this postseason.
Díaz had a slightly better outing Wednesday (one scoreless inning) after his disastrous Sunday performance of five earned runs in 0.2 innings.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are on track to win the NL West and probably earn a first-round bye in the postseason. That comes despite a recent onslaught of injuries. Los Angeles is not unaccustomed to a stacked injury list, but the Dodgers' elite depth — aided by a top-ranked farm system and unrivalred spending power — makes them uniquely resilient.
What has helped L.A. win back-to-back World Series titles, however, is their knack for getting healthy at the right time and charging into October at full strength. The Dodgers are hoping to do just that, again. Let's rank six potential returners who could make an outsized impact.
6. RHP Edwin Díaz
Should Edwin Díaz actually come back for the playoffs? He got rocked in his recent Triple-A rehab appearance. The Dodgers' prized $69 million investment has only pitched 13.2 innings in the majors this season, with a disastrous 11.85 ERA (not a typo). Díaz has not looked right at any point.
While the Dodgers presumably want such an expensive and accomplished reliever on the postseason roster, it may be smarter to punt on this season entirely. Díaz is more than capable of rebuilding confidence and getting healthy in the offseason, but it's unclear if L.A. can rely on him in even the lowest-leverage spots currently. Rather than playing with fire, so to speak, the Dodgers should probably lean on their spectacular bullpen depth and keep Díaz on the sidelines. The risk far outweighs the potential reward of rushing him back.
That said, when healthy, Díaz has a long track record as one of MLB's best closers. We know he can electify in the late innings. If the Dodgers are confident for reasons we on the outside aren't privy too, never say never on a triumphant turnaround.
5. RHP Roki Sasaki
Through two seasons, the Rōki Sasaki experience has not quite lived up to expectations for Dodgers fans. Hailed as the best Japanese pitching prospect in a generation, the 24-year-old looks an awful lot like... a prospect. A work in progress. Los Angeles expected immediate results. Now, the Dodgers are hoping Sasaki can iron out command issues against MLB competition. He appeared briefly in the minors this season, but the Dodgers are effectively all-in on Sasaki as a major league pitcher.
Sasaki is expected to recover from a blister before the playoffs, although the Dodgers are uncertain about his exact role. The rotation is much too deep for Sasaki to start in a must-win environment. He was effectively L.A.'s closer last October — a role in which he thrived — but a healthy Tanner Scott removes Sasaki from consideration for that role. Expect him in the bullpen, probably handling bulk work if one of L.A.'s starters is forced out early.
4. C Dalton Rushing
Dalton Rushing was recently returned to the IL after suffering a setback in his recovery from UCL surgery. He's done catching for the season, but L.A. still hopes the 25-year-old can return as a hitter. Of course, if Rushing is effectively relegated to DH, it will be hard to get him in the lineup with Shohei Ohtani also on the roster. Rushing could end up as a situational, pinch-hitter type in October, if he's even on the roster.
It's a credit to how deep the Dodgers are that Rushing being "situational," rather than essential, is even in the cards. The rookie backstop cooled off after the All-Star break, but he's still phenomenally talented. He has a .798 OPS and 120 wRC+ as a rookie, with 12 home runs in only 250 at-bats.
Rushing is stuck behind Will Smith on the org chart, which complicates his future somewhat, but the Dodgers will find ways to use him if he's available.
3. RHP Edgardo Henriquez
The Dodgers hope Edgardo Henriquez can return from a low-grade back strain come the playoffs. The 24-year-old fireballer has quickly established himself as one of baseball's most dominant relievers. He has a 2.85 ERA and 1.03 WHIP with 71 strikeouts in 60.0 innings pitched this season; he ranks in MLB's 99th percentile for both hard-hit rate (27.1 percent) and average fastball velo (100.8 mph).
Henriquez is more than a hard-thrower. He misses barrels and limits explosive hits, able to force groundballs or lifeless bloopers just as often as he forces swing-and-miss. He leans heavily on his four-seam and sinker combo, with a sweeping slider that leaves opposing hitters gasping for air (.191 xwOBA). Should Henriquez return in time, the Dodgers can plug him right into high-leverage spots and expect results. He's the real deal, folks.
2. OF Andy Pages
Andy Pages is back in the batting cage after breaking his hand in mid-August. The Dodgers' centerfielder has enjoyed a proper breakout campaign, posting a .797 OPS and 119 wRC+ with elite defensive metrics and 12 stolen bases. In terms of fWAR, or wins above replacement, Pages ranks third among L.A. positional players (3.9), behind only Shohei Ohtani (6.8) and Max Muncy (4.0).
The Dodgers really need Pages on cleanup duty in centerfield. He covers so much ground and features a killer arm, which wipes runs off the board. Pages' bat cooled down before the injury, but he's still far more dangerous than L.A.'s alternatives — although the recent promotion of top prospect Josue De Paula does create a difficult decision for manager Dave Roberts, assuming the DH spot reverts back to Ohtani.
Speaking of which...
1. DH Shohei Ohtani
This was obvious, yeah? Shohei Ohtani is currently on ice as he attempts to shed bicep and knee problems. That said, the Dodgers plan to get him back before the regular season ends — and it would be absolutely shocking if Ohtani weren't leading off in Game 1 of the Dodgers' first postseason series.
The nagging nature of Ohtani's injuries mean he won't take the mound again in 2026, but he's still the most valuable hitter in the majors, on balance. Yes, Yordan Álvarez and Pete Crow-Armstrong are enjoying better seasons, but Ohtani is the man you want at the plate in a big spot. Drafting a fantasy team, he's your No. 1 pick. So on and so forth.
After spending the early portion of his MLB career on an unserious Angels team, Ohtani is two-for-two in the World Series since joining the Dodgers. He has consistently come up large in the playoffs. Assuming Ohtani is anywhere close to 100 percent, the Dodgers are once again (easy) favorites to win it all.

CINCINNATI (AP) — Elly De La Cruz hit a two-run homer and the Cincinnati Reds at least temporarily prevented the Los Angeles Dodgers from clinching the NL West title with a 6-2 victory on Wednesday night.
The Dodgers (92-60) needed a win or a loss by San Diego to win their fifth straight NL West crown and 13th in 14 seasons. The Padres played at Colorado later Wednesday.
Left-hander Blake Snell started for the Dodgers but departed after one inning with left groin tightness. Snell, who threw a no-hitter for the Giants in his last appearance in Great American Ball Park, faced three batters, allowing a hit with a strikeout on 19 pitches.
Blake Treinen took over in the second as the first of six relievers used by Los Angeles.
Mookie Betts singled off Andrew Abbott in the third and scored on Will Smith's double to put the Dodgers ahead 1-0. Abbott allowed a run on three hits with five walks in 4 2/3 innings. Tejay Antone (3-2), the third of six Cincinnati pitchers, got the last out of the sixth.
De La Cruz's homer off Seth Halvorsen (1-2), his 28th of the season, put the Reds ahead 2-1 in the third. It was De La Cruz's fifth longball against the Dodgers this season, most of any opposing player.
Dane Myers' homer off Bobby Miller, his seventh, extended the Reds' lead to 3-1 in the fifth.
Juan Brito's RBI single made it 4-2 in the sixth.
TJ Friedl singled with the bases loaded in the seventh to drive in two runs. Sal Stewart was thrown out at the plate by Dodgers center fielder Tommy Edman to end the inning.
The Dodgers stranded 12 runners and went 0 for 11 with runners in scoring position.
Up next
RHP Brady Singer (6-14, 5.38 ERA) will start Thursday's series finale for the Reds. The Dodgers had not announced their starter.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to win their series against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday.
The Dodgers took Monday's series opener, 4-1, behind seven shutout innings from Tarik Skubal. Then, they won Tuesday's game, 4-0, behind seven shutout innings from Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
On Wednesday, LA has another superstar pitcher on the mound in left-hander Blake Snell.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going [Wednesday] — you feel good about preventing runs,” manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
Dodgers vs Reds Pitching Matchup on Wednesday
Snell is looking to continue his run of dominance since returning from midseason elbow surgery.
The left-hander has gone 4-0 with a 1.04 ERA across six starts, striking out 46 while allowing zero home runs over 34.2 innings of work.
Snell, who pitched 5.2 innings in his most recent start, is still looking to go deeper into games moving forward. He hasn't pitched more than six innings in any of his six starts.
“I mean the goal, at worst is definitely six for me,” Snell said. “I also know that I can go seven, eight, nine. I know I’m able to do it. So for me not to, I just have to get more efficient early in the game. I feel like once I get past the first couple innings, I start cruising and start figuring it out."
Opposite Snell will be left-hander Andrew Abbott, who's 6-11 with a 4.78 ERA and 120 strikeouts over 154.1 innings this season.
He's allowed seven earned runs in two of his last three starts, and has a 7.71 ERA since the start of August.

This article is a part of Verducci’s View, a new weekly baseball newsletter from Sports Illustrated senior writer Tom Verducci. Every Monday, Tom empties out his notebook over email and covers MLB’s hottest topics, provides in-depth analysis through both text and video breakdowns, looks forward to what’s worth watching during the week and more. If you want to be featured in his new mailbag, please email newsletters@si.com with any questions about MLB or his decades in the sport.
📺 Breakdown of the Week
One of the many fascinating revelations Tarik Skubal shared with me for our upcoming SI cover piece was how he puts his entire trust in his catcher when it comes to pitch selection. That approach becomes more interesting when you change teams midseason. Skubal had more catchers in his first seven starts with the Dodgers (Hunter Feduccia, Ben Rortvedt and Will Smith) than he did in his previous 70 starts with the Tigers (Dillon Dingler and Jake Rogers).
A pattern has emerged in how the Dodgers’ catchers call pitches for Skubal as compared to the Tigers’ choices: he is leaning more into his changeup (his best pitch) and backing off his sinker (his fourth best pitch). He threw more changeups in his first month with Los Angeles (179) than he did in any month in his career. As the following chart shows, his use of his changeup has risen from 25.1% to 28.8%.
Skubal’s tweak to his arsenal as a Dodger is even more interesting when you dive into what he throws when he’s in trouble. With the Tigers, Skubal threw his four-seamer more than any other pitch with runners in scoring position (37%). With the Dodgers, the changeup has been his No. 1 choice with RISP (36%).
Skubal Pitch Choice with RISP, 2026
| Pitch Type | Tigers | Dodgers | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Four-seam fastball | 37% | 33% | -4% |
| Changeup | 29% | 36% | +7% |
| Slider | 14% | 14% | - |
| Sinker | 20% | 14% | -6% |
| Curveball | 1% | 3% | +2% |
Like the Rays, the Dodgers believe in leaning into your best pitch, especially in tight spots. How good is Skubal’s changeup? It has the highest whiff rate of any changeup in MLB (46.8%). It also is among the very best at getting out of jams:

| Pitcher | No. of Changeups | BA |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Bradgley Rodriguez, Padres | 162 | .108 |
| 2. Tarik Skubal, Doders | 121 | .128 |
| 3. Martin Perez, Braves | 186 | .132 |
| 4. Eduardo Rodriguez, D-Backs | 174 | .133 |

Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor arrived in the big leagues in 2015 as a premier defender with questions about how much pop he had in his bat. Across 416 minor league games he hit just 23 home runs and slugged .387.
Eleven years later, Lindor is one of the greatest power hitting shortstops in the history of the game who is on the Hall of Fame highway. His career slugging in the majors is .472, behind only Joe Cronin (.475) among shortstops with at least 1,500 games at the position.
His next home run will be career No. 300. He will become only the 27th player with 300 home runs and 200 stolen bases, but the first with 1,500 games at shortstop.
Lindor has hit 292 of his home runs while playing shortstop, tying him with Miguel Tejada for third on the all-time list and within range of passing Alex Rodriguez (344) and Cal Ripken Jr. (346) to become the all-time home run leader while playing shortstop.

Mookie Betts and Kiké Hernández wore No. 21 Los Angeles Dodgers jerseys against the Cincinnati Reds on Tuesday night as part of Major League Baseball celebrating Roberto Clemente Day, which is observed every Sept. 15.
MLB permits nominees and previous recipients of the Roberto Clemente Award to wear a No. 21 jersey, and Betts was the winner of last year’s honor. Puerto Rican natives are also allowed to wear the number in honor of Clemente, which Hernández again took advantage of.
Will Smith is the Dodgers’ nominee for this year’s Roberto Clemente Award, and while he did not play in the team’s 4-0 win over the Reds, it also appears he didn’t elect to wear No. 21. Both Betts’ and Hernández’s transaction pages listed them as wearing the number, while Smith’s page still showed him wearing his usual No. 16.
Betts went 0-for-4 with a strikeout against the Reds. Hernández, like Smith, did not appear in the Dodgers’ victory.
The Roberto Clemente Award is presented annually in recognition of the Major League player who best represents the game of baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions, both on and off the field.
The concept of honoring Major League players for their philanthropic work was created in 1971 as the “Commissioner’s Award.” The recognition was renamed to the “Roberto Clemente Award” in 1973 as tribute to Clemente following his passing while delivering relief supplies for earthquake victims in Nicaragua on Dec. 31, 1972.
“I was obviously too young to remember Roberto Clemente, but from the people that I respect and what he was as a person, certainly supersedes what he was as a ballplayer, which says a lot,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said on SportsNet LA.
“Just unfortunately way too young. It’s very cool that young players, current players, understand who Roberto Clemente was and they have that award every year. It’s a big feather in everyone’s cap. Baseball is certainly better with Roberto Clemente.
“I met his family in Pittsburgh, so that was pretty cool. Been to the Roberto Clemente museum in Pittsburgh, which was great for me as well.”
How to vote Will Smith for Roberto Clemente Award
Fans can now vote for the Roberto Clemente Award winner via MLBTogether.com/clementeaward (in both English and Spanish). Fan voting extends through the final day of the regular season on Sunday, Sept. 27. The winner of the fan vote will count as one vote among those cast by the blue-ribbon panel.
The league-wide winner of the Roberto Clemente Award will be honored at the 2026 World Series following selection by the aforementioned panel. It includes representatives from the commissioner’s office, Capital One, MLB-affiliated networks (MLB Network, FOX Sports, ESPN and TBS), MLB.com, National Baseball Hall of Fame, as well as Roberto’s children, Enrique, Luis and Roberto Clemente, Jr.
Smith is looking to become the fifth player in Dodgers franchise history to win the honor. Previous recipients include Betts (2025), Justin Turner (2022), Clayton Kershaw (2012) and Steve Garvey (1981).

Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman has been battling right knee pain, but the worst of it may be behind the team’s contact specialist.
Entering Tuesday’s game, Freeman was on a 3-for-30 cold streak and had missed three of the last six games because of his knee issue.
Things looked shaky for Freeman, who has built a reputation as one of baseball’s most consistent players.
However, he put together his best game in weeks, going 3-for-5 on singles, but showing the elite bat-to-ball skills that make him a candidate to bat around .300 year in, year out.
After the game, manager Dave Roberts noted that Freeman looked more like himself.
“It looked good,” Roberts said. “It looked more like Freddie.”
Freeman had asked Roberts before the game, jokingly, if he could play on Wednesday, a scheduled day off, if he got three hits.
As a result of Freeman’s performance, the manager is allowing Freeman to skip an off-day on Wednesday and play again, with the infielder eager to get the ball rolling.
“I feel like my faults are I try to hit the ball to the opposite field too much, and I let the ball get too deep,” he said.
“So today was [get the] foot down early, catch the ball out front a little bit, and it kind of worked. I wasn’t squaring the ball up in the game, but I’ll take those three hits and keep that work going tomorrow, and hopefully we’ll get hot.”
What does Freeman’s uptick mean for the Dodgers?
With the best rotation in baseball, the Dodgers are left scrounging around for offense any way that they can find it.
Teoscar Hernandez, Josue De Paula, and Mookie Betts have been the most consistent sources, with Max Muncy and Will Smith in the picture as well.
Still, the Dodgers need as many players in a spot as possible to deliver timely hits, and Freeman’s experience and skills make him a clear-cut candidate to step up.
To deliver results quickly, as he manages his knee and struggles, Freeman has made a mechanical change, getting out in front of the ball to catch it earlier on his bat.
The result may be less clean contact and hard hits, but more consistent contact, with the idea that it makes him valuable come the postseason.
“I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable,” he said. “I’m trying to find something that works for four weeks.”
Freeman has the right approach to deliver just what the Dodgers need. The entire offense does not need to be excellent; simply being good enough will lead to a three-peat.

Los Angeles Dodgers newest star pitcher Tarik Skubal reveals the impact of Will Smith calling his pitches.
Smith has come back from his neck injury and made an immediate impression on the pitching staff.
Skubal, who joined the team at the trade deadline, hasn’t been able to work much with Smith since Smith’s injury.
However, since coming back to the Dodgers on September 1st, Smith has caught three games for Skubal and left the two-time Cy Young winner quite impressed.
In those three starts, he has a 1.80 ERA over 20 innings with four walks and 20 strikeouts.
Most notably, in his last start, Skubal went seven innings, allowing no runs, one walk, and nine strikeouts in what became the best start of his Dodgers career.
After the game, Skubal told reporters that Smith called every pitch, never shaking him off once during the outing.
“Yeah, I think it’s just kind of reading, reacting to what situations, or reading swings,” Skubal said.
“And honestly, a lot of that’s Will. Like, I trust him with calling every pitch. I think I shook one time tonight, so we’re in pretty good rhythm.”
How Smith is helping Skubal settle in with the Dodgers
Skubal has said he’s been thinking too much about pitch selection rather than focusing on execution, leading to inconsistent results.
Since joining the Dodgers, Skubal has felt he underestimated how much familiarity with the catchers and other members of the pitching staff matters.
Now, he is working hard to focus on that line of communication.
“I think just trying to get on the same page with everybody here, you know, catching department, pitching department, constantly learning each other and developing those relationships,” Skubal explained.
“And I probably underestimated that a little bit, but just communicating, having open dialogue with all these guys on what I like to do, what I’m comfortable with.
“And then, honestly, some things I’m uncomfortable with, working on those things because it’s gonna be important.
“I think we’re developing a really good relationship and rhythm, just with me and everybody else, the catchers and the pitching department.”
With Skubal settling in and starting to make the most out of a pitching operation that has succeeded over the last several years, this bodes very well for the postseason outlook.

CINCINNATI –– Every day, Tarik Skubal learns something new about playing for the Dodgers.
Monday's lesson: Clinching a playoff spot warrants only subtle celebrations.
"It's different than anything I've experienced, for sure," Skubal chuckled on Monday night, after the Dodgers recognized their 14th consecutive postseason berth with only a subdued postgame champagne toast and brief speech from manager Dave Roberts.
"But," the club's new star pitcher added, "I think it just speaks to the people in this room and what they expect out of this team. That was cool. A little toast and move on. Forget it happened. We've got more to accomplish this season."
Consider it the latest step in Skubal's acclimation process with the Dodgers –– another little moment that made him feel more at home with his new team.
He's now six weeks on from his emotional trade from the Detroit Tigers at the deadline.
And he's starting to find a comfort level that, after an uneven start to his Dodgers tenure, is helping him look more like the star pitcher he is accustomed to being.
"Constantly learning each other and developing relationships –– a lot of that stuff you don't realize, no one writes about that kind of relationship –– but I think it matters, it matters a lot. I probably underestimated that a little bit," said Skubal, who had spent the entirety of his career in Detroit before his marquee move to the Dodgers.
"But just communicating, having an open dialogue with everyone, all these guys, on what I like to do, what I'm comfortable with and honestly what I'm uncomfortable with … I think we're developing a real good relationship," he added.
And as a result, as manager Dave Roberts noted, "I think the last couple [outings he has made] have been his best."
That was certainly true on Monday, when Skubal spun a gem with the Dodgers' postseason berth in the balance.
He delivered his first scoreless start with the team by blanking the Reds over seven innings at Great American Ball Park. He gave up just three hits and one walk while striking out nine batters in a 90-pitch domination.
"To take the mound on the night that we had a chance to clinch, and we did it," Roberts said, "I think that's something he should be proud of."
More important to Skubal was the way it reflected his growing familiarity with the Dodgers' catchers and pitching department.
He noted he only shook Will Smith off one time all night. He praised the rhythm he has developed with pitching coaches in pre-game prep meetings. And he credited it all with helping him eliminate some perfectionist tendencies that hampered his first month with the team (when he gave up nine runs in 24 innings while lacking the ruthless efficiency that made him a reigning back-to-back Cy Young Award winner).
"I think a lot of the struggles have been 'me vs. me,' thinking too much out there and not competing the way I know how to compete," Skubal said. "Sometimes I try to be too perfect with things instead of just attacking guys over the middle of the plate and letting my stuff play, especially early in games, behind in the count, just not trying to be too fine."
To put it more simply, Skubal added, it was a process of "trying to find the rhythm of who I know I am."
And to people around the team, it's no coincidence that has happened as he's carved out a place in his new clubhouse, as well.
"He's just chill," pitching coach Mark Prior said. "You can joke around with him. You can talk to him."
Few players have grown closer with Skubal than Blake Snell to this point. They've sat side-by-side in the dugout during games, locked in constant conversation. They were pulling practical jokes on one another Tuesday, knocking over each other's chairs in the clubhouse. They've even begun making Step Brothers-inspired jokes about being new best friends on social media.
"I think we're best friends," Snell deadpanned. "Some days, he agrees."
Snell told the California Post that their relationship blossomed naturally, with Snell immediately being struck by how Skubal was "very confident and very secure with who he is" even amid new surroundings.
Two other observations:
"I didn't think he was that funny," Snell joked, describing a side of Skubal that came out Monday night when he razzed backup catcher Hunter Feduccia about a snazzy short-sleeve dress shirt and matching pair of brown slacks ("Outfit of the day!" Skubal declared).
"And," Snell added, "I like how competitive he is. Because it just makes both of us so much better."
That latter dynamic could fuel the Dodgers' entire rotation moving forward, especially entering a postseason in which the group will likely have to carry the team.
"Every time one of our boys go, we want them to dominate, and then the next man up wants to do even better," Snell said. "I think that's very important, to know that we're supporting each other and we're pushing each other to be great, and that we're not focused on just our own achievements. We're focused on our group of starting pitchers all succeeding."
Prior echoed those sentiments, noting that with Skubal specifically: "He wants to have fun. And he wants to win."
Lately, Skubal has been, now on a four-start stretch with only five runs allowed in his last 26 innings.
For the Dodgers, it's a sign of his growth process since being acquired by the club; one that could prove crucial in their three-peat ambitions.
"It's hard to get in that rhythm [and develop] that trust," Roberts said. "But for me, I see just more of the trust in whatever is called, and then you can just go out there [be himself]."

LOUISVILLE, Ky. — Louisville native Will Smith, who played baseball at Kentucky Country Day and the University of Louisville, is the city’s newest recipient of a Hometown Hero banner.
Smith’s banner was unveiled on Tuesday, Sept. 15, at Grocers Ice Lofts at 609 E. Main St. in downtown Louisville.
Currently, a catcher with the Los Angeles Dodgers, Smith is a three-time World Series champion. He and the Dodgers won the championship on Nov. 2, 2025, after he hit a go-ahead home run against the Toronto Blue Jays.
Smith was drafted by the Dodgers in the first round of the 2016 MLB Draft, going 32nd overall. He made his debut with the team in May 2019.
While at Kentucky Country Day, Smith hit .528 with 11 home runs, 36 RBIs and 24 stolen bases, according to his MLB biography. He also went 7-1 with a 0.87 ERA and 100 strikeouts. While at the University of Louisville, Smith started all three seasons, finished his collegiate career as the 2016 team captain and earned All-ACC Third Team honors.
Smith is married and is the father of two daughters. Smith founded the Catching Hope Foundation, which is focused on providing better opportunities for kids in the Los Angeles and Louisville communities.
The Greater Louisville Pride Foundation announced in 2025 that Smith would receive a banner. He is one of seven new banners announced.
